title: Overlooking the One Thing That Changes Everything
speaker: Aaron Brockett
goal: Tonight, we aim to confront the personal 'one thing' each man might be holding onto that prevents him from fully following Jesus, prompting genuine self-assessment and actionable steps by next week.
scripture_instructions: Assign two readers. First reads verses 13-22, focusing slowly on the rich young ruler's question and Jesus' response. Second reads verses 23-31, emphasizing Jesus' message about wealth and salvation.

icebreakers.label: A
icebreakers.question: What's one item you'd struggle to lend out to someone and why?
icebreakers.note: This question eases into the evening's theme by discussing personal attachments to possessions.

icebreakers.label: B
icebreakers.question: Describe a time when holding onto something ultimately held you back.
icebreakers.note: Encourages sharing personal narratives of struggles with letting go.

icebreakers.label: C
icebreakers.question: What's a comfort you prioritize that you're ashamed to admit?
icebreakers.note: Prompting vulnerability about personal comforts can mirror deeper spiritual dependencies.

sections.title: The Rich Young Ruler
sections.setup: In Mark 10:13-22, a young man approaches Jesus with a sincere question about inheriting eternal life. This man, though adhering to the commandments, misses the one thing Jesus knows holds his heart, his possessions. Jesus invites him to sell all and follow, exposing a tough truth about reliance and true discipleship.

questions.ask: When have you relied on accomplishments or rule-following for identity rather than your relationship with God?
questions.lead: The rich young ruler believed his achievements and adherence to the law made him 'enough' in God's eyes.

questions.ask: Who are you reluctant to confront truthfully due to comfort or fear of conflict?
questions.lead: Jesus looked at the man and loved him, despite knowing his heart's conflict.

questions.ask: What have you chosen over a deeper commitment to Christ?
questions.lead: The young man walked away sad, choosing wealth over discipleship.

questions.ask: When have you tried to achieve something that should have been received freely?
questions.lead: The rich man's question was sincere yet revealed a misunderstanding of inheritance.

questions.ask: What is the most difficult thing you need to let go of to follow Jesus more fully?
questions.lead: Jesus asked the man to give up everything to follow Him.

reflection_questions: When have I relied on accomplishments or rule-following for identity rather than my relationship with God?
Who am I reluctant to confront truthfully due to comfort or fear of conflict?
What have I chosen over a deeper commitment to Christ?
When have I tried to achieve something that should have been received freely?
What is the most difficult thing I need to let go of to follow Jesus more fully?

sections.title: Jesus' Hard Teachings
sections.setup: In verses 23-27, Jesus speaks to the disciples about the difficulty for the wealthy to enter God's kingdom, using the metaphor of a camel and the eye of a needle. This shocks the disciples, prompting a revelation about possibilities with God versus human achievement.

questions.ask: Where are you attempting to earn God's favor rather than relying on His grace?
questions.lead: Jesus emphasizes that human effort cannot earn entrance into God's kingdom.

questions.ask: What teachings of Jesus have you found most challenging to accept or implement in your life?
questions.lead: The disciples were amazed at the standard Jesus set and questioned who could be saved.

questions.ask: How have you witnessed God making the impossible possible in your life?
questions.lead: The impossibility of salvation through human means is only made possible with God.

questions.ask: What does your attitude towards money reveal about your heart's priorities?
questions.lead: Jesus uses wealth to illustrate deeper heart issues.

reflection_questions: Where am I attempting to earn God's favor rather than relying on His grace?
Which teachings of Jesus have I found most challenging to accept or implement in my life?
How have I witnessed God making the impossible possible in my life?
What does my attitude towards money reveal about my heart's priorities?

sections.title: Surrender and Reward
sections.setup: In verses 28-31, Peter reminds Jesus that the disciples have given up everything to follow Him. Jesus assures them of the sure rewards for sacrifices made in His name, reinforcing that the first will be last and the last first, highlighting the upside-down nature of God's kingdom.

questions.ask: What sacrifices have you made for your faith, and what have been the personal costs and rewards?
questions.lead: Peter highlights the sacrifices made by the disciples.

questions.ask: Can you recall a time when giving up something for God led to unexpected blessings?
questions.lead: Jesus speaks of receiving a hundredfold for those who have left everything for His sake.

questions.ask: How do you navigate the tensions between sacrifice and the persecutions that may follow?
questions.lead: Jesus' promise of rewards comes with the inclusion of persecution.

questions.ask: Where might you be clinging to status or recognition, and how can you shift those priorities?
questions.lead: Jesus' teaching flips human notions of greatness and reward.

reflection_questions: What sacrifices have I made for my faith, and what have been the personal costs and rewards?
Can I recall a time when giving up something for God led to unexpected blessings?
How do I navigate the tensions between sacrifice and the persecutions that may follow?
Where might I be clinging to status or recognition, and how can I shift those priorities?

closing_go_around: Each man names the 'one thing' revealed to him tonight that he needs to surrender and states a specific, actionable step to achieve this before we meet again.
prayer: Each man prays a simple sentence asking for strength to surrender his 'one thing,' and the leader closes by reading through the promises found in Matthew 6:19-21 about treasures in heaven.

cheat_sheet.response: Prompt again with 'What about this struck a chord with you?'
Refocus on the question by linking back to the passage's key themes.
Invite another perspective by asking, 'Does anyone have a different take?'
Request deeper reflection with, 'How does that specifically play out for you?'
Acknowledge it quietly, ask if they're okay, and offer the group to wait and extend grace.
Steer back with, 'Let's make sure we're tying this to the passage and our lives directly.'

key_themes: Possessions and Discipleship: The tension between worldly wealth and following Jesus wholeheartedly.
Grace over Achievement: Salvation is received, not achieved, underscoring the importance of grace.
Personal Surrender: Identifying and surrendering the 'one thing' that might hinder spiritual growth.
Divine Possibility: Recognizing that with God, what seems impossible to us is made possible.
Reward and Sacrifice: Jesus' assurance of eternal rewards to those who sacrifice for His kingdom.
commitment_prompt: Identify the 'one thing' to surrender this week, and commit to sharing your progress with your accountability partner, stating their name and how they'll help keep you on track.
leader_notes: Aaron opened with a powerful illustration of the Challenger disaster, pointing out how a small oversight led to catastrophic failure. This story framed the sermon by illustrating how something seemingly minor, when overlooked, can result in massive consequences. The rich young ruler had everything outwardly but missed the critical internal change, just as NASA ignored the critical warning about the O-ring.

The passage in Mark 10 captures a moment when Jesus exposes the limitations of human achievement in favor of divine grace. Jesus asked the rich young man to let go of his wealth, not as a rejection but as a love-driven invitation to true discipleship. Aaron's focus was on the contrasting ideas of doing to earn versus receiving through grace.

Tonight's guiding thesis is that the 'one thing' we often hold is what holds us back. Follow the sermon’s three-part outline: the confrontation of reliance on possessions (verses 13-22), the difficulty of kingdom entry for the self-reliant (verses 23-27), and the promised reward of surrender (verses 28-31). Each section encourages a fresh confrontation with what we might avoid releasing.

For this group of high-functioning men, polished answers can mask deeper resistance to change. Lean into the personal, pressing them to identify the 'one thing' they are clinging to. Tonight earns its keep in the section on surrender, where vulnerability around letting go of control or status might emerge.

First, someone might feel shame over financial struggles or past decisions. Approach this with sensitivity, providing one-on-one space later if needed. Second, if someone’s one thing isn't material wealth but personal status or emotional security, allow room for that to surface. Third, be ready for emotional responses when discussing past sacrifices or failures; the go-around should help process discomfort constructively.
